G-computation decomposition of the average treatment effect

Source: R/gcomp.R
bic_gcomp.Rd

Estimates the average treatment effect and its exact decomposition into a discrete-component contribution (through the boundary probabilities) and a continuous-component contribution (through the conditional mean), Proposition 2.3 (one boundary) / Proposition 2.4 (two boundaries) of Ospina (2026). Identification rests on the ordinary potential-outcomes assumptions (SUTVA, ignorability given the covariates in fit, positivity); this function does not check them.

Usage

bic_gcomp(fit, treat, data, weights = NULL)

Arguments

fit

A fitted model from bic_fit().

treat

Character, the name of the treatment variable.

data

The data frame the effect is averaged over (by default, the data fit was fitted on).

weights

Optional averaging weights (e.g. survey weights), normalized internally to sum to one. Defaults to equal weights.

Value

A named numeric vector c(tau, tau_alpha, tau_mu), with tau_alpha + tau_mu == tau exactly (to floating-point precision).

Details

Reading the three numbers: tau is the total change in the mean response caused by treatment. tau_alpha is the part of that change coming from treatment moving units onto or off the boundary (a change in how many units attain the inflated value); tau_mu is the part coming from treatment shifting the conditional mean among units that remain in the interior. They can have the same sign (both mechanisms reinforcing) or opposite signs (one mechanism offsetting the other, so that tau alone understates how much is actually happening); only the three-number decomposition distinguishes these cases, since tau by itself looks the same either way when the components happen to be small, and looks deceptively modest when they are large and opposed.

Examples

dat <- simulate_bic(400, seed = 1)
fit <- bic_fit(y ~ T + W2, nu.formula = ~ T + W1, data = dat)
bic_gcomp(fit, "T", dat)
#>         tau   tau_alpha      tau_mu 
#>  0.04459171 -0.07564943  0.12024114 
attr(dat, "truth")
#> $tau
#> [1] 0.04490327
#> 
#> $tau_alpha
#> [1] -0.08649041
#> 
#> $tau_mu
#> [1] 0.1313937
#>
